name: FM18W08-SGTR
title: FM18W08: 256-Kbit (32 K × 8) wide-voltage bytewide F-RAM
summary: A 32 K × 8 nonvolatile ferroelectric RAM with an SRAM-style parallel bus and the standard 28-pin 32 K × 8 SRAM/EEPROM pinout, running from 2.7 V to 5.5 V over –40 °C to +85 °C. Writes complete at bus speed with no delay or polling, endurance is 10^14 cycles and data is kept 151 years at 65 °C. Each access is started by a falling edge on CE, which latches the address; access time is 70 ns and cycle time 130 ns at 3.0–5.5 V. FM18W08-SGTR is the 28-pin SOIC on tape and reel.

circuits.title: Pull-up resistor on CE
circuits.description: A microcontroller or microprocessor drives the address, data and control lines of the F-RAM directly. A resistor from CE to VDD holds the chip disabled while the controller's pins float in reset, so CE rises and falls with VDD through each power cycle and no access happens below 2.7 V.

parts.note: Pull-up; low enough in value that CE tracks VDD up to a valid HIGH, high enough that the current drawn while CE is LOW is small.

notes: U1.VDD and U1.VSS join the system supply and ground.

circuits.title: Pull-up resistor on WE, CE tied to ground
circuits.description: With CE grounded the chip is always enabled, so WE must stay HIGH through power cycles or data is corrupted. A resistor from WE to VDD keeps it there while the controller's pins float in reset; the controller drives OE, the address and the data bus.

parts.note: Pull-up; low enough in value that WE tracks VDD up to a valid HIGH, high enough that the current drawn while WE is LOW is small.

operation.text: 32,768 bytes of ferroelectric RAM addressed by A14–A0 over an SRAM-style parallel bus. The array is built of rows 64 bits (8 bytes) wide; each new row starts on an 8-byte address boundary.

operation.topic: Every cycle starts on CE falling
operation.text: Unlike an SRAM, the part needs a falling edge on CE to begin each access. That edge latches the address, after which the address lines may change once the hold time tAH is met without disturbing the cycle. Once begun, a cycle runs to completion inside the part even if CE goes HIGH early. CE must also not stay LOW past its maximum LOW time.

Each memory cycle is an access followed by pre-charge. Pre-charge starts when CE goes HIGH and needs CE HIGH for at least tPC. Because of it, the cycle time (130 ns at 3.0–5.5 V) is longer than the access time (70 ns).

Data appears after the access time. DQ is driven only while OE is LOW and the data is valid: taking OE LOW early does not put invalid data on the bus, which avoids current spikes. With OE HIGH the bus stays high impedance.

Writes take the same time as reads and are nonvolatile the moment they finish: there is no write delay and no need to poll for completion, so any read or write can follow straight away. In a CE-controlled write WE is already LOW when CE falls, the cycle is a write from the start and DQ is never driven, whatever OE does. In a WE-controlled write CE falls first, the cycle begins as a read with DQ driven per OE, and WE falls later. Either way the address latches on CE falling, the write ends on whichever of WE or CE rises first, the access time must be met before that, and data must be stable for tDS before it.

Every read or write uses one endurance cycle of a whole 8-byte row, since the cell is read and then restored. Spreading frequently used data over different rows makes the rated 10^14 cycles last longer; at that rating one row can be accessed 150,000 times a second for over 20 years.

CE cannot be held grounded as with an SRAM that is accessed by changing the address alone: each new address needs its own LOW-going CE strobe, which both latches it and gives the HIGH time for pre-charge. When porting a design, the memory controller's address and control timing is the thing to check; often the CE strobe is the only change.

The part does not lock out access at low supply as a battery-backed SRAM does; it accepts access anywhere in the 2.7 V to 5.5 V operating range, and the system must stop the processor reaching it when VDD is out of range. Holding the processor in reset through power-down may be enough. CE should be pulled HIGH so it tracks VDD through power-up and power-down, keeping the part deselected below 2.7 V. If CE is tied to ground instead, WE must not be LOW during power cycles, or data is corrupted; a pull-up on WE serves. After VDD reaches its minimum the first access waits tPU (10 ms), and VDD ramps no faster than 30 µs/V up or down.
